# spacc

*species accumulating in the neighbourhood*

<!-- badges: start -->
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/spacc)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=spacc)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/gcol33/spacc/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/gcol33/spacc/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/gcol33/spacc/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/gcol33/spacc)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
<!-- badges: end -->

spacc builds species accumulation curves that add sampling sites in the order of their distance from a starting point, such as plots added one by one outward from a point in a survey region, and shows how the curve changes with that point.

The classical curve of `specaccum()` in [vegan](https://vegandevs.github.io/vegan/) adds sites in random order, without using their spatial arrangement. spacc samples a focal point in continuous space, ranks every site by its distance from that point and counts the new species along the ranking. It repeats this from many focal points in C++ with RcppParallel, so the curve carries a confidence ribbon showing how richness depends on where the expansion begins. spacc also computes the random-order curve, so you can compare the two and judge how much the spatial arrangement of your sites matters.

spacc supports:

- **Seven expansion orders.** Fixed-focus nearest neighbours (`knn`), nearest-centroid expansion (`kncn`), a nearest-neighbour walk (`nn_walk`), distance- and direction-weighted growth (`gaussian`, `cone`), the classical random order (`random`) and the data order (`collector`).
- **Diversity beyond richness.** Hill numbers, beta diversity with turnover and nestedness, coverage-based rarefaction, and phylogenetic and functional diversity accumulate along the same spatial order; [`spaccHill()`](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/reference/spaccHill.html) is the entry point.
- **Geographic coordinates.** `distance = "haversine"` works on longitude and latitude with no projection step, and an sf polygon through `focal_domain` restricts the focal points to a known study boundary.
- **Large site sets.** Above 500 sites the nearest-neighbour methods switch from a distance matrix to a k-d tree from [nanoflann](https://github.com/jlblancoc/nanoflann), or a ball tree for haversine distances ([Methods and Algorithms](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/theory.html#the-two-tier-traversal-backend)).
- **Fitting and comparing curves.** [`extrapolate()`](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/reference/extrapolate.html) fits asymptotic richness models, including Michaelis-Menten, Lomolino, Weibull, logistic and extreme value models, and `compare()` tests two curves by permutation, bootstrap or area under the curve.

Existing curves from `vegan::specaccum()` enter through `as_spacc()`, so they share the plotting and comparison methods. Each method follows a published definition, listed with its reference in the DESCRIPTION and in [Methods and Algorithms](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/theory.html), and a methods section can cite those papers for the estimators and spacc for the spatial ordering.

## Installation

Install the released version from CRAN. Windows and macOS get a binary that needs no build tools:

```r
install.packages("spacc")
```

The development version compiles C++ code. Install the build tools for your operating system first:

| Operating system | Build tools |
|---|---|
| Windows | [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) matching your R version |
| macOS | Run `xcode-select --install` in Terminal |
| Debian / Ubuntu | Install `r-base-dev` |

Check that R can find the compiler:

```r
pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)
```

Then install spacc from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/spacc")
```

The build needs GNU make and a C++17 compiler, which the build tools above provide. The nanoflann library ships as a header inside the package, and RcppParallel brings its own threading library, so no system libraries are needed.

## Usage

1. Build a spatial accumulation curve with `spacc()` from a site-by-species matrix and the site coordinates.
2. Build the random-order curve with `method = "random"` and test the difference with `compare()`.
3. Fit an asymptote with `extrapolate()`, or follow other diversity measures with `spaccHill()` and `spaccBeta()`.

The input is a matrix or data frame with one row per site and one column per species, holding presence-absence or abundance, and the site coordinates as a data frame with columns `x` and `y` or an sf object of points. Coordinates are planar by default; `distance = "haversine"` reads `x` and `y` as longitude and latitude in degrees.

In the example below, each of 40 species occurs around its own position along the x axis, so neighbouring sites share species:

```{r spacc, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Species accumulation curve rising from about 10 species at one site to all 40 species at around 150 sites, with a green band showing the 95% interval of the curves from 50 focal points"}
library(spacc)

set.seed(1)
coords <- data.frame(x = runif(200), y = runif(200))
centres <- runif(40)
prob <- outer(coords$x, centres, function(x, m) exp(-(x - m)^2 / 0.02))
species <- matrix(rbinom(length(prob), 1, prob), nrow = 200)

sac <- spacc(species, coords)
plot(sac)
```

The line is the mean over 50 focal points, and the ribbon holds 95% of the curves from single focal points.

Adding the sites in random order instead reaches the species far faster, because it ignores that neighbouring sites share species:

```{r compare}
sac_random <- spacc(species, coords, method = "random")
compare(sac, sac_random)
```

## Diversity beyond richness

Each diversity function carries the spatial ordering through to a different measure, with `map = TRUE` for per-site values and `as_sf()` for GIS output:

```r
hill <- spaccHill(species, coords, q = c(0, 1, 2), map = TRUE)
plot(hill, type = "map", q = 0)

beta <- spaccBeta(species, coords, index = "sorensen")
plot(beta, partition = TRUE)
```

[Diversity Accumulation](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/diversity.html) covers Hill numbers, the alpha, beta and gamma partition, and phylogenetic and functional diversity.

## Grouped and spatiotemporal accumulation

`groups` splits the species into groups, such as native and alien species or families, and accumulates each under the same spatial site order. `time` adds a temporal axis to the distance, weighted against space with `w_space` and `w_time`:

```r
sac_grouped <- spacc(species, coords, groups = status, seed = 42)
plot(sac_grouped, facet = TRUE)

sac_st <- spacc(species, coords, method = "nn_walk",
                time = site_years, w_space = 1, w_time = 0.5)
```

[Community Assembly and Turnover](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/community-assembly.html) applies grouped curves to community structure.

## Documentation

Start with [Getting Started with spacc](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/quickstart.html): one path from a site-by-species matrix to spatial and random-order curves, their comparison and extrapolation.

- [Diversity Accumulation](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/diversity.html): Hill numbers, beta diversity, phylogenetic and functional accumulation.
- [Extrapolation and Species-Area Models](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/extrapolation.html): asymptotic models and total richness beyond the sampled sites.
- [Richness Estimation and Completeness](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/richness-estimation.html): total richness from frequency counts and sample completeness.
- [Rarefaction and Standardization](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/rarefaction-standardization.html): curves standardized to common effort or coverage.
- [Spatial Analysis: Endemism, Fragmentation, and SAR](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/spatial-analysis.html): endemism-area curves, fragmentation and species-area relationships.
- [Community Assembly and Turnover](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/community-assembly.html): grouped curves, turnover and null models of the sampling design.
- [Methods and Algorithms](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/articles/theory.html): the expansion methods, distance metrics and nearest-neighbour backends.
- [Full reference](https://gillescolling.com/spacc/reference/): every function, grouped by job.
